Question about the Tom Clancy Humble Bundle... why would I pay $10 instead $8.48?
To be clear the 2 extra games are not highly rated compared to others in the series.

To be fair. Splinter Cell: Blacklist was shaping up to be an excellent game until they patched it for PvP and broke the single player save feature. I was too busy to get back to it and see if it had been fixed.

Back to the question...are we really asking why you'd pay an extra $1.51 on a bundle that supports charity? That's not enough to buy a short Starbucks drip coffee. There's a fine line between discerning and cheap. Sometimes the best thing we can do is stop and ask ourselves which side of that line we're on.

I should be clear. I'm not trying to promote cheapness as much as I'm sitting there questioning the order of the game choices.

I would think you would put the best games at the higher end to make it more desirable to pay more.

$1.51 isn't a lot, but in comparison to paying just a dollar for the first 5 games... which has the beta, and then if you wish getting 5 more games... I'd just think they'd make it more motivating to spend the extra 1.51....

"Best" is a pretty subjective term. You're getting two additional games for $1.51, one of which is worth 15-20 times as much quite handily (Splinter Cell: Blacklist is still $30 on Steam). Why do we need to worry about which game is providing incentive to spend an extra $1.51? You could pay $30 for the bundle, tell yourself you bought SC: Blacklist and got everything else free, and the question of incentive and "best" never even enters into it. Hell, you might even forget that you're supporting charity.

Some things in life warrant asking, "why?" Only some things.

Given how many charities have shown themselves to be corrupt over the years I'm not sure it's quite that simple. It's virtually impossible to know which charities are legitimate anymore. For example, I used to think Amnesty International was doing really good work and I'd contribute on a regular basis, then they were exposed. I had basically been paying for an executive's posh living/retirement fund while they were performing a fraction of the work they were taking credit for.
Given the number of charities that are doing good work and managing their resources responsibly, pointing to the corrupt ones as justification to discount the honest ones is a cop-out.
My point is entirely that it's very difficult to know which ones are the honest ones. You'd know this if you bothered to read my post past the first sentence.

So what? We're not discussing whether the charities you can support through the Humble Bundle are reliable. We're talking about whether or not two additional games justifies an extra $1.51 cost for a package where some of the monies raised go to support charity. We don't need to haul it off on some personal tangent.
